steps.text: **The opposition.** Two kings stand on one file (or rank) with exactly one square between them. Kings may never touch, so the side to move must step aside and give ground. Having the opposition means the *other* side is to move. It is a position plus a turn: the same placement can be a win or a draw, depending on whose turn it is.

steps.text: **Why it works.** Kings can never touch, so each one takes squares from the other. The king to move must give way, and the other king then steps forward or takes the opposition back. That costs the mover only when the other side has a pawn to protect and a king ahead of it. [I] Calling the move a burden is a rule of thumb: with the pawn far ahead of the defender, or spare pawn steps in hand, having the move can be fine.

steps.text: **Key squares.** With the pawn on its fourth rank, the three squares two ranks in front of it are **key squares** (for the e-pawn: d6, e6 and f6). A king on one wins when the defender cannot capture the pawn at once. [I] This is a rule of thumb read from tablebase-checked boards; the board after the three examples shows an exception. The opposition is a method: it forces the other king aside so yours can reach a key square.

steps.text: **What the defender can do.** There are two defences in the middle of the board. First, if the attacking king is only level with the pawn, take the opposition yourself. Second, stay in front of the pawn and keep a square between the kings. Both need exact timing, so each gets a board. The corner is a third, separate resource and comes with the edge pawn later.

steps.text: **Three ways to explain the same thing.** Capablanca taught the opposition as a rule about the move. Edward Lasker named the moment the pawn reaches its sixth rank as critical and showed that a spare pawn move can take the opposition back. Nimzowitsch thought the usual account vague and preferred forcing the enemy king to yield. [S] All three are paraphrased from our reading sheets. [I] They look like one idea seen from three sides: the king not on the move owns the better squares.

**Remember.** The opposition means the two kings face each other with one square between them and the other side must move. Ask who is to move, and whether my king is ahead of the pawn. It wins when the stronger king reaches a key square. It fails when the defender's king is level with the pawn or already attacks it, and then it is only a draw.
